passage:
Lavanya: Did Rakesh say anything about the promotion?
Zeenat: Not yet. I'm being patient
Lavanya: It's been fourteen months
Zeenat: Good things come to those who wait
Lavanya: Have you asked him?
Zeenat: I don't want to seem pushy. He'll get to it
Lavanya: And you're still doing his extra reports?
Zeenat: Yes, till things settle down
Lavanya: Patience is waiting while you do something. This is just waiting
Zeenat: Ouch
Lavanya: Sorry. I care. Could you ask for a short chat and ask what the criteria are?
Zeenat: My stomach hurts thinking about it
Lavanya: Practise on me tonight?
Zeenat: ...ok 🙂

qa.q: How long has Zeenat been waiting for news of the promotion?
qa.a: Fourteen months.

qa.q: What is Lavanya feeling as Zeenat keeps calling it patience?
qa.a: Lavanya is concerned and a little frustrated, but caring. Lavanya says sorry for the bluntness and adds 'I care'.

qa.q: What small step does Lavanya suggest?
qa.a: Ask Rakesh for a short chat and ask what the criteria for the promotion are, and practise the conversation first.

qa.q: What might Zeenat be afraid of?
qa.a: Seeming pushy or hearing an answer Zeenat does not want, since Zeenat's stomach hurts at the thought of the conversation.

grounding: A person calls waiting for a promotion patience while avoiding a needed conversation.

passage:
In the small-town market, Kishore had watched his neighbour Gautam wait eleven months for his cousin Anil to apologise over a broken shop agreement. "I'm being patient," Gautam said whenever the name came up. Every festival he laid an extra plate for Anil, and every festival it stayed empty. He began taking the long way to avoid Anil's shop.
Kishore noticed Gautam's tight jaw and that he had never once said, "That hurt me."
One evening over tea Kishore said, "Patience has a limit. Is it patience if you're avoiding the conversation?"
Gautam stared at his glass. "I'm scared Anil will say no."
"Then at least you'd know," said Kishore.
Gautam nodded slowly. "Sunday," he said.

qa.q: How many months has Gautam waited for the apology?
qa.a: Eleven months.

qa.q: What is Kishore feeling and thinking about Gautam's waiting?
qa.a: Kishore is worried and honest. Kishore notices the tight jaw and the avoidance and suspects the patience is really avoiding the conversation.

qa.q: What turning point did Kishore's question bring?
qa.a: Kishore asked whether it was patience if Gautam was avoiding the conversation, and Gautam admitted fear and decided to go on Sunday.

qa.q: What might Gautam be afraid of?
qa.a: Gautam is afraid that Anil will say no, which is why he has waited instead of asking.

grounding: A person waits for an apology, calling it patience, while avoiding a needed conversation.

passage:
In the café near their office in Dubai, Layla listened as Noa said it again. "I'm being patient. The promotion will come."
It was the third year Layla had heard this. Noa had never once asked the manager what it would take. At every review Noa smiled, said "fine", and came back to complain.
Layla stirred her coffee. "Can I say something? I don't think it's patience anymore. Patience is when you've asked and you're waiting for the answer. You haven't asked."
Noa looked stung. Then quiet. "I'm scared he'll say no."
"Then you'd know," Layla said gently. "And you could decide."
The next week Noa booked fifteen minutes with the manager. Layla didn't ask how it went. Noa told her anyway, grinning: "He gave me a list."

qa.q: For how long had Noa been waiting for the promotion?
qa.a: Three years.

qa.q: What was Layla feeling as Noa said it again?
qa.a: Layla felt concerned and a bit frustrated, hearing the same line for the third year.

qa.q: What distinction did Layla draw?
qa.a: Patience is waiting after you've asked; Noa hadn't asked, so it had become avoidance rather than patience.

qa.q: What was Noa afraid of?
qa.a: Noa was scared the manager would say no.

grounding: Shows an observer noticing a friend call years of waiting for a promotion patience while avoiding the needed conversation.

passage:
At the design office, Baljeet had watched Raghav go quiet for two months. In March their team lead, Mr Sen, had presented Raghav's layout to the client as his own. Raghav said nothing. "I'm being patient," he told Baljeet. "He'll realise and apologise."
He hadn't. Raghav now ate lunch alone, skipped team meetings when he could, and flinched when Mr Sen passed his desk.
One evening Baljeet sat on the edge of Raghav's desk. "Waiting only works if he knows there's something to wait for. Does he?"
Raghav hesitated. "Probably not."
"Then maybe it's not patience. Maybe you're avoiding the talk."
The next morning Raghav asked Mr Sen for ten minutes. He came back pale but lighter. "He said he hadn't thought about it. He's going to credit me in the next client email."

qa.q: When did Mr Sen present Raghav's layout as his own?
qa.a: In March.

qa.q: What did Baljeet feel watching Raghav over two months?
qa.a: Baljeet felt worried, seeing Raghav eat alone, skip meetings and flinch whenever Mr Sen passed.

qa.q: What question helped Raghav see his waiting differently?
qa.a: "Waiting only works if he knows there's something to wait for. Does he?"

qa.q: How did Mr Sen respond when Raghav finally spoke?
qa.a: Mr Sen said he hadn't thought about it and agreed to credit Raghav in the next client email.

grounding: Shows an observer seeing a colleague wait for an apology, calling it patience while avoiding a needed conversation.

passage:
Dear Ganga Masi,
You asked about Meher. It's been a year since her sister said those awful things at the wedding, and Meher still says she's "being patient", waiting for an apology. But she has never told her sister she was hurt. She just goes silent at family dinners and leaves early.
Last week I finally asked her, gently, "How long will you wait? And does she even know?" Meher cried. She said she was scared that if she brought it up, it would all blow up.
I told her real patience might mean saying it once, calmly, and then giving her sister time. She's thinking of writing her a letter.
I don't know if it will work. But waiting forever without a word wasn't working either.
Love,
Arohi

qa.q: How long has it been since the wedding?
qa.a: A year.

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling when finally asking Meher?
qa.a: Arohi felt concerned and gentle, worried that Meher's silence was hurting more than helping.

qa.q: What did Arohi suggest real patience might look like?
qa.a: Saying the hurt once, calmly, then giving the sister time, perhaps through a letter.

qa.q: Why had Meher avoided raising it?
qa.a: Meher was scared that bringing it up would make everything blow up.

grounding: Shows an observer noticing a friend call a year of silent waiting for an apology patience, while avoiding the needed talk.

passage: You know Gargi from my team, right? I'm Anjali, the one who sits across from her, and I've watched this for two years now. Every appraisal cycle Gargi says, "I'm being patient, they'll notice." She stays late, fixes everyone's slides, never asks for anything. Last March the lead role went to someone who joined after her. She smiled through the cake cutting, then sat in the parking lot for an hour. I sat there with her. She said, "Good things come to people who wait." And I kept thinking, but you're not waiting for anything, you're hiding from one conversation. Last week I finally said it: "Waiting works once you've asked. Have you asked?" She went very quiet. Then she booked twenty minutes with our manager for Friday. Honestly, I'm nervous for her.

qa.q: What does Gargi say every appraisal cycle?
qa.a: She says, "I'm being patient, they'll notice."

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling while watching Gargi keep waiting?
qa.a: Anjali felt worried and a bit frustrated, seeing that the waiting was really a way to avoid one conversation, and now feels nervous for Gargi before Friday.

qa.q: What could Gargi bring to the Friday meeting to make it useful?
qa.a: She could say plainly that she wants the lead role, ask what she needs to show to get it, and agree on a date to check back.

qa.q: How might Gargi see her own long wait?
qa.a: She probably sees it as a quiet strength, so hearing it called hiding may have stung before it pushed her to book the meeting.

grounding: Shows a teammate noticing that a colleague's long wait for promotion is avoidance of a needed conversation rather than active patience.
